A wheeled vehicle that moves independently, with at least three wheels, powered mechanically, steered by a driver and mostly for personal transportation but relatively smaller than a truck/lorry and a bus.
A type of motor vehicle designed to move on the ground under its own stored power and intended to carry a driver, a small number of additional passengers, and a very limited amount of other load.
A heavier four-wheeled (normally horse-drawn) vehicle designed to carry goods (or sometimes people). [from late 15th c.]
A (mostly four-wheeled) lighter vehicle chiefly designed to transport people, generally drawn by horse power.
(countable, legal) A written order, issued by a court, ordering someone to do (or stop doing) something.
(archaic, or, literary) A wagon; a four-wheeled cart for hauling loads, usually pulled by horses or oxen.
(historical, originally) A light two- or four-wheeled carriage with a folding top, pulled by a single horse.
To treat as a brother.
In a state of marriage; having a wife or a husband.
An act of rotating one's body 360 degrees in the backward direction.
(also dairy products or dairy produce) Products produced from milk.
Happening or occurring during daylight, or primarily active during that time.
A conventional phrase used to start a letter or conversation or otherwise to acknowledge a person's arrival or presence.
The act of congratulating.
A type of small fish, Carassius auratus, typically orange-colored.
A long dowel or plank protruding from the ground; a fencepost; a lightpost.
Originally, a stick; now specifically, a long and slender piece of metal or (especially) wood, used for various construction or support purposes.
(heraldiccharge) A vertical band down the middle of a shield.
A large post, often used as supporting architecture.

A tall, slim post or tower, usually tapering upward, used to support, for example, sails or observation platforms on a ship, the main rotor of a helicopter, flags, floodlights, meteorological instruments, or communications equipment, such as an aerial, usually supported by guy-wires (except in the case of a helicopter).
A stake driven into the ground.
Straightforward; not evasive; candid and direct.

As purchased or as commonly available, without modification or customization.
A fine fiber excreted by the silkworm or other arthropod (such as a spider).
Synonym of silky, like silk, silklike, particularly
The fourth largest city in Kosovo, and the seat of its eponymous municipality and district.

A grammatically complete series of words consisting of a subject and predicate, even if one or the other is implied. In modern writing, when using, e.g., the Latin, Greek or Cyrillic alphabets, typically beginning with a capital letter and ending with a full stop or other punctuation.
The sediment at the bottom of a liquid, or from which a liquid has been filtered.
(archaic, chiefly, in the plural) Dregs, sediment.
The sediment settled at the bottom of a liquid; the lees in a container of unfiltered wine.
The state, quality, or the fact of being eligible.
Considering; taking into account.

A country consisting of a main island, the island of Tasmania and other smaller islands, located in Oceania; historically, a collection of former colonies of the British Empire. Official name: Commonwealth of Australia. Capital: Canberra.
Of, from, or pertaining to Australia, the Australian people or Australian languages.
Any cup-shaped or bowl-shaped tool, usually with a handle, used to lift and move loose or soft solid material.

A hand tool with a handle, used for moving portions of material such as earth, snow, and grain from one place to another, with some forms also used for digging. In strict usage differentiated from a spade, which is designed solely for small-scale digging and incidental tasks such as chopping of small roots.
two-handed, single-bladed oar
A garden tool with a handle and a flat blade for digging. Not to be confused with a shovel which is used for moving earth or other materials.
(nautical) Any of the triangular blades at the end of an anchor, designed to catch the ground.

Any of several usually relatively thin, rigid, flat, or sometimes curved surfaces radially mounted along an axis, as a blade in a turbine or a sail on a windmill, that is turned by or used to turn a fluid.

A type of lever used to propel a boat, having a flat blade at one end and a handle at the other, and pivoted in a rowlock atop the gunwale, whereby a rower seated in the boat and pulling the handle can pass the blade through the water by repeated strokes against the water's resistance, thus moving the boat.
The part of a lute-type string instrument, such as a guitar, that holds the tuning pegs or tensioning screws of the strings.
Strong affection.
The lowest side of a triangle or other polygon, or the lowest face of a cone, pyramid or other polyhedron laid flat.
The bottom surface of a natural structure, entity, or space (e.g. cave, forest, ocean, desert, etc.); the ground (surface of the Earth).
In a vector space, a linearly independent set of vectors spanning the whole vector space.
The bottom or plantar surface of the foot.
The base or foot of a column, statue, vase, lamp.
A floor.
The number of distinct symbols used to represent numbers in a particular base, as ten for decimal.
To make known.
To observe, to take account of.
To point out; to discover; to direct to a knowledge of; to show; to make known.
a pipe

An insect, Daktulosphaira vitifoliae of the family Phylloxeridae (not the genus Phylloxera), that is very destructive to grape vines; also, the diseased condition of a vine caused by this insect. [from 19th c.]
A grouping of all the members of a legislature from the same party.
The act of consuming or destroying.
Without meaning to, in an unintentional manner, not intentionally.
With little enthusiasm or interest.
Able to be carried or easily moved.
Habitually travelling from place to place.
A group of people organized for some common purpose, usually of about ten members.
A comic originating in Japan.

A Christian feast commemorating the resurrection of Jesus Christ. It is celebrated on the first Sunday (and Monday) following the full moon that occurs on or next after the vernal equinox, ranging in most of Western Christianity (such as Protestantism and Roman Catholicism) from March 22 to April 25, and in Eastern Christianity (such as the Coptic Church and Eastern Orthodox Church) from April 4 to May 8.
An image, often a photographic negative, produced by radiation other than visible light; especially an X-ray photograph.
A vertical (or nearly vertical) rock face.
The process of making or growing worse, or the state of having grown worse.
Hell; the bottomless pit; primeval chaos; a confined subterranean ocean. [First attested around 1350 to 1470.]
A deep, steep-sided rift, gap or fissure; a gorge or abyss.
A very steep cliff.
(archaic) A rocky shelf or ledge of a cliff, a mountain, etc.
(geology) A cliff at the edge of a plateau or ridge caused by erosion or faulting; the steeper side of an escarpment.
Wood that has been pre-cut and is ready for use in construction.
Wood sawn into planks or otherwise prepared for sale or use, especially as a building material.
A group sharing common characteristics, such as the same language, law, religion, or tradition.
A long-standing group of people sharing cultural aspects such as language, dress, norms of behavior and artistic forms.
A small mindless sketch, etc.
(arts) An image of the outline of an object.
Falsifications or misrepresentations intended to disparage or discredit another.
The ordinal form of the number one hundred.
Divided into a hundred parts.
The legal right to take care of something or somebody, especially children.
A pulley suspended on a cable mounted on an incline, designed to enable a user to travel from one point to another by means of gravity.
A system of suspended cables from which cable cars are hung.
A country's entire maritime military force, including ships and personnel.
A piece of art that depicts the sea or shoreline.

A brief explanatory note or translation of a foreign, archaic, technical, difficult, complex, or uncommon expression, inserted after the original, in the margin of a document, or between lines of a text.
A notice requesting a postponement of a court proceeding.
A restatement of a text in different words, often to clarify meaning or from memory rather than verbatim.
An animal that leads.
Lacking the degree of ability and responsibility necessary to do a task successfully.
Not able to do something; not proficient; displaying incompetence.
Of a person or workforce: not having a skill or technical training.
Having no talent or natural ability.
Having a weak or indecisive character; ineffectual or dim-witted.
A deviation from a rule or from what is regarded as normal; an outlier.
An ancient Greek philosopher, logician, and scientist (382–322 BCE), student of Plato and teacher of Alexander the Great.
The act or an instance of repeating or being repeated.
Resolute or strenuously active.
Very hot; burning, scorching; also, glowing with heat.
Showing strong feelings; passionate; forceful or intense.
One who attends to the maintenance of a building and provides services to its tenants and visitors.

An unwillingness to settle for anything less than perfection.
Containing sarcasm.
A sweet popular in the Indian subcontinent, made by deep-frying a maida flour batter and soaking it in sugar syrup.
Not pleasant.
